details:
**Thus Spoke Zarathustra (Also sprach Zarathustra)**
Nietzsche's philosophical novel (1883–1885) about a prophet named after Zoroaster, the founder of Zoroastrianism. It opens with Zarathustra descending from his mountain cave after ten years of solitude, meeting an old saint in the forest, and preaching in a marketplace where a tightrope walker falls after being startled by a jester. Other episodes include the fable of the spirit's three metamorphoses (camel, lion, child) and Zarathustra's animals, an eagle with a serpent coiled around its neck.

**"God is dead"**
Nietzsche's most famous proclamation, which appears most prominently in the "Parable of the Madman" in The Gay Science. A madman with a lantern announces in a marketplace that "God is dead... and we have killed him." It describes the collapse of belief in God as a foundation for European values.

**Übermensch (Overman or Superman)**
The ideal figure introduced in Thus Spoke Zarathustra, who creates his own life-affirming values beyond conventional Christian morality. Zarathustra describes man as "a rope, tied between beast and Übermensch," a bridge rather than an end in itself.

**On the Genealogy of Morals (Morality)**
Nietzsche's 1887 work of three essays tracing the origins of moral values. It argues that a "slave revolt in morality," driven by ressentiment, reversed noble values, equating powerlessness and meekness with goodness. It includes the parable of lambs who call birds of prey "evil," the "blond beast," the "breeding of an animal with the right to make promises," and a critique of the ascetic ideal promoted by priests.

**Master morality and slave morality**
Nietzsche's contrast between two value systems. Master morality, held by the noble and strong (such as the Romans), sorts actions into "good" and "bad," while slave morality, which he associated with Judaism and Christianity, sorts them into "good" and "evil" and praises humility and weakness. He develops the idea in Beyond Good and Evil and the Genealogy.

**Eternal recurrence**
The thought experiment that one's life will repeat in exactly the same way infinitely. In The Gay Science a demon steals into your loneliest loneliness and announces that you will live this life again innumerable times. It is central to Thus Spoke Zarathustra, where Zarathustra is at first horrified by the thought that even mediocre man will recur.

**The Gay Science**
Nietzsche's 1882 work, whose title comes from a Provençal expression for the art of poetry. It contains the Parable of the Madman, the first statement of eternal recurrence, and the image of the Buddha's shadow still shown in a cave long after his death.

**Beyond Good and Evil**
Nietzsche's 1886 book, which opens with "Supposing truth is a woman, what then?" Its first section, "On the Prejudices of Philosophers," asks why we value truth rather than untruth. It also says that "every profound spirit needs a mask" and presents the "will to power" as the basic drive behind all life.

**The Birth of Tragedy**
Nietzsche's first major book (1872), which argues that Greek tragedy arose from the fusion of two artistic impulses: the Apollonian (order, form, clarity, dream) and the Dionysian (frenzy, intoxication, the dissolution of the self).

**Ecce Homo**
Nietzsche's autobiography, completed in 1888 just before his mental collapse, with grandiose chapter titles like "Why I Am So Wise," "Why I Am So Clever," "Why I Write Such Good Books," and "Why I Am a Destiny (Fatality)." It begins "Above all, do not mistake me for someone else" and ends with "Dionysus versus the Crucified."

**Will to power**
Nietzsche's idea that the basic drive behind all living things is a striving to grow, expand, and dominate, rather than mere survival. He wrote that "this world is the will to power—and nothing besides!" Nazi propagandists distorted the concept.

**Amor fati ("love of fate")**
The attitude of embracing everything that happens, including suffering, as necessary. In Ecce Homo, Nietzsche calls it his "formula for greatness in a human being." It is closely tied to saying "yes" to life and to eternal recurrence.

**The Antichrist**
Nietzsche's 1888 polemic against Christianity, which he accuses of promoting weakness and "otherworldly hopes" that devalue this life. It criticizes Ernest Renan's portrayal of Jesus as a "genius," discusses the "redeemer type," and calls for a "revaluation of all values."

**Twilight of the Idols**
An 1888 work subtitled "How to Philosophize with a Hammer," in which Nietzsche "sounds out" old idols. It contains the line "without music, life would be a mistake" and a section tracing how the "true world" (Plato's Forms, Kant's noumena) finally became a fable.

**Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche and the horse in Turin**
Nietzsche's sister, who controlled his literary estate after his 1889 breakdown and edited his unpublished notes (as The Will to Power) to suit her nationalist and antisemitic views. According to legend, his breakdown began in Turin when he threw his arms around a horse that was being whipped.
